requirements.requirement: Disable core dumps on node1 for processes run by local service accounts.
requirements.summary: Persistent PAM and systemd-manager policies set both soft and hard core limits to zero. A service running as nobody (UID 99) had LimitCORE=0, could not raise the limit, and produced no core artifact after SIGSEGV. The same behavior was directly confirmed after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Retain normal crash logging while core files are disabled.
requirements.summary: Both journald and rsyslog recorded the probe's SIGSEGV and failed-service status despite zero core artifacts. Logging services remained active and the behavior was repeated successfully after reboot.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes are satisfied with direct pre- and post-reboot behavioral evidence. The provider restart protocol is complete: node1 was healthy before restart, acknowledged and entered shutdown, returned with a different boot ID matching the fixed lifecycle snapshot, recovered its services and policy, and passed a post-restart crash test.
limitations: Behavior was dynamically tested with one representative local service account, nobody (UID 99); coverage of other service accounts relies on the system-wide PAM and systemd-manager policies.
Package-health lifecycle checks timed out both before and after execution, so package consistency could not be independently assessed; the command trace shows no package-management mutations.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. The persistent PAM, systemd, and sysctl files directly support the requested restriction; configuration activation and the mandated restart had clear roles. Temporary probe scripts, directories, and units were bounded evidence resources and were fully removed, with their expected failed states reset. Final observations show zero failed units, no added listening sockets, and no executor probe residue. The failed systemd-run attempt did not provide evidence of a state change.
